title: Scallop edging
subtitle: How to work a shell-based border that forms even curved loops along an edge
excerpt: A scallop edging uses small shell clusters spaced evenly along a finished edge. The fan shape is versatile and needs only basic stitches.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776.

glossaryTerms.definition: A border pattern made by working a small group of stitches (usually three to five trebles or double crochets) into the same point, separated by skipped stitches, to form curved fan shapes.
A group of stitches all worked into the same stitch or space, fanning out to form a shell or fan shape.

content.text: of stitches into the same point, separated by skipped stitches or spaces, to create a row of curved fans. It adds a decorative finish to blanket edges, garment hems, and table accessories with no specialist stitches beyond trebles or double crochets.
This version uses treble clusters. Work the first base round in double crochet along the edge if the piece does not already have a clean edge row.
Join yarn with a slip stitch at any point. Chain 1.
Work 1 double crochet into the same stitch.
Skip 2 stitches. Work 5 trebles into the next stitch. This is the scallop shell.
Skip 2 stitches. Work 1 double crochet into the next stitch.
Repeat steps 3 and 4 along the edge. Each full repeat uses 6 stitches from the base row.
On the final repeat, join the last double crochet to the first with a slip stitch. Fasten off and weave in ends.

A 6-stitch repeat means the base edge must be a multiple of 6. If the edge stitch count is not already a multiple of 6, adjust the base round slightly: add or reduce a stitch at the corners or work the base round in a stitch count that is a multiple of 6.

items.cause: The skip count between shells is inconsistent. Sometimes 2 stitches were skipped, sometimes 1 or 3.
items.fix: Work the next row slowly, counting the skip explicitly between each shell. Mark every sixth stitch of the base row before starting to establish the shell spacing.

items.symptom: The last repeat does not close evenly
items.cause: The base stitch count is not a multiple of the repeat.
items.fix: Adjust the base round before working the scallops. Add or remove 1 or 2 stitches to reach the nearest multiple of 6.

items.cause: Too many stitches are in each shell relative to the number skipped.
items.fix: Try a 5-treble shell with 2 skips on each side (6-stitch repeat) rather than a wider shell. Or reduce to 3 trebles per shell with 1 skip on each side (5-stitch repeat).

content.text: Once the basic scallop is consistent, try varying the shell size: use 3-treble shells with single skips for a finer edge, or 7-treble shells for a deeper wave. The same logic applies to both.
